articles.title: UN leaders renew push to defeat racism, 25 years after Durban
articles.summary: “No country is free of racism.” That warning from US youth activist Marley Dias set the tone on Monday as UN Member States reinvigorated global efforts against racism, discrimination and xenophobia with a new declaration.
articles.content:
What you need to know

The new declaration will be submitted for formal adoption at the General Assembly

Adopted in South Africa in 2001, the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action is a blueprint for stamping out racism, discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance

From a rise in racist speech, to calls for reparations for colonialism and slavery, delegates lauded progress so far – but underscored the work ahead

Follow our live coverage of the day-long high-level meeting here

During the meeting, Ms. Dias, founder of #1000BlackGirlBooks, urged States to confront the enduring legacies of slavery, colonialism and discrimination, emphasising many young people have never been taught the histories that shaped the institutions and societies they inherited.

Recalling that she launched #1000BlackGirlBooks when she was 11 – because she could not find girls like herself in books at school – she underscored the power of representation and education.

Further, youth must be central to full implementation of the Durban Declaration, she said, including through accurate and accessible digital educational materials.

“Let’s write a new chapter together,” she said.

Landmark blueprint

The 2001 adoption of the Durban Declaration followed widespread and grave concern over entrenched racism since the UN’s inception, from colonialism to 46 years of South African apartheid.

The United Nations and the international community are continuing to work towards dismantling systemic racism to establish dignity, equality and justice for all.

Here are some highlights:

1948: Declaration of Human Rights

1963: UN Declaration on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination

1978: First World Conference to Combat Racism and Racial Discrimination

New tech threats

During the day-long meeting on Monday, some delegates pointed to new and emerging challenges. Voicing deep concern over “the alarming resurgence of all forms of racism”, the representative of Uruguay, speaking on behalf of the Group of 77 and China, called on States to combat racism, hate speech and religious intolerance, both online and offline.

Social media enables messages of hatred to spread “at alarming speed”, alongside information and disinformation increasingly amplified by artificial intelligence (AI), she said.

While new technologies can be “extremely beneficial for sustainable development if used responsibly”, countries must work together to ensure that technological developments “contribute to a better world and do not perpetuate or exacerbate existing and structural inequalities”.

Calls for slavery reparations

Some delegates called for reparations for slavery and colonialism. Adam Tesfaye Abera, Chief of Staff at Ethiopia’s Foreign Affairs Ministry, reaffirmed the country’s commitment to its Programme of Action, highlighting the urgent need for reparations for colonialism and the transatlantic slave trade.

Riyad Mansour, Permanent Observer for the State of Palestine, said the Durban Declaration was a reminder that colonialism, genocide, apartheid and slavery have profound and lasting consequences and that “historical injustice cannot be overcome through remembrance alone, it requires justice and reparation”.

The declaration carries particular significance for Palestinians, Mr. Mansour said, recalling that 25 years ago it expressed concern over their plight under foreign occupation and recognised their right to self-determination and an independent State.

Defeating ‘poison’ of racism

The UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for stronger laws, inclusive institutions and reparatory justice to combat racism – a “poison” rooted in slavery and colonialism that is still potent today.

The Secretary-General highlighted discrimination faced by people of African descent as well as Indigenous Peoples, migrants, refugees and minorities.

Around the world, “racism continues to poison societies, deepen inequalities and deny people their fundamental rights and freedoms,” he said.

‘Antidote’ to a toxic legacy

Pointing out that it “is deeply rooted in the entrenched legacies of colonialism, enslavement and oppression”, Mr. Guterres said racism takes many forms, from economic, social and political inequalities, both within and across countries, to discriminatory laws, policies and institutions.

Moreover, digital tools and technologies “are amplifying the spread of hate speech and disinformation, perpetuating lies and harmful stereotypes, and fuelling violence and abuse,” he warned.

“The antidote to these poisons is unity and tangible action,” he said.

Reject injustice, support change

In this regard, the UN chief called for making concrete change during the Second International Decade for People of African Descent, which began in December 2024.

“And we need to see the universal ratification and full implementation of the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination,” he added.

“Together, let’s reject injustice,” he said. “Together, let’s build societies where racism and discrimination have no place – today and for all time.”

articles.personality_title: UN renews global effort to fight racism 25 years after Durban
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In 2001, the United Nations adopted the Durban Declaration to fight racism, discrimination, and xenophobia worldwide. This was a response to long-standing problems like colonialism and apartheid, especially in South Africa. Over 20 years later, racism remains a serious issue, and the UN is updating its commitment to end it.

**What happened** – On Monday, UN Member States gathered to renew their efforts against racism with a new declaration. US youth activist Marley Dias spoke about how many young people never learn the true history of slavery and colonialism. She highlighted the importance of education and representation, sharing how she started the #1000BlackGirlBooks campaign at age 11 because she couldn’t find books about girls like her. The meeting also discussed new challenges like racist hate spreading quickly online, especially with new technologies like artificial intelligence.

**Impact** – This renewed declaration is important because it acknowledges that racism is still widespread and changing with new technology. It also calls for specific actions like reparations for slavery and colonialism, stronger laws, and education for young people. The inclusion of youth voices and focus on digital tools show a modern approach to tackling racism. The meeting reminded countries that racism harms many groups, including people of African descent, Indigenous Peoples, migrants, and refugees.

**What's next step** – The new declaration will be formally adopted at the UN General Assembly. The UN Secretary-General called for countries to ratify and fully implement the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination. The UN will also focus on the Second International Decade for People of African Descent starting in December 2024, aiming to make real changes in laws and institutions to stop racism.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The United Nations is renewing its global fight against racism with a new declaration that emphasizes education, reparations, and stronger laws to build fairer societies.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’ONU relance la lutte mondiale contre le racisme 25 ans après Durban
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En 2001, l’Organisation des Nations Unies a adopté la Déclaration de Durban pour combattre le racisme, la discrimination et la xénophobie dans le monde. Cela répondait à des problèmes anciens comme le colonialisme et l’apartheid, notamment en Afrique du Sud. Plus de 20 ans plus tard, le racisme reste un problème sérieux, et l’ONU renouvelle son engagement pour l’éradiquer.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Lundi, les États membres de l’ONU se sont réunis pour renouveler leurs efforts contre le racisme avec une nouvelle déclaration. La militante américaine Marley Dias a expliqué que beaucoup de jeunes ne connaissent pas l’histoire vraie de l’esclavage et du colonialisme. Elle a souligné l’importance de l’éducation et de la représentation, racontant qu’elle a lancé la campagne #1000BlackGirlBooks à 11 ans parce qu’elle ne trouvait pas de livres sur des filles comme elle. La réunion a aussi abordé les nouveaux défis, comme la propagation rapide des discours de haine en ligne, notamment avec l’intelligence artificielle.

**Impact** – Cette nouvelle déclaration est importante car elle reconnaît que le racisme est toujours présent et évolue avec la technologie. Elle appelle à des actions précises comme des réparations pour l’esclavage et le colonialisme, des lois plus fortes, et une éducation pour les jeunes. L’inclusion des jeunes et l’attention portée aux outils numériques montrent une approche moderne pour combattre le racisme. La réunion a rappelé que le racisme affecte de nombreux groupes, notamment les personnes d’ascendance africaine, les peuples autochtones, les migrants et les réfugiés.

**Prochaine étape** – La nouvelle déclaration sera officiellement adoptée lors de l’Assemblée générale de l’ONU. Le Secrétaire général a appelé les pays à ratifier et appliquer pleinement la Convention internationale sur l’élimination de toutes les formes de discrimination raciale. L’ONU se concentrera aussi sur la Deuxième Décennie internationale pour les peuples d’ascendance africaine à partir de décembre 2024, pour apporter des changements concrets dans les lois et institutions afin de stopper le racisme.

**Une phrase pour retenir** – L’Organisation des Nations Unies renouvelle sa lutte mondiale contre le racisme avec une nouvelle déclaration qui met l’accent sur l’éducation, les réparations et des lois plus fortes pour construire des sociétés plus justes.
articles.personality_title_es: La ONU renueva el esfuerzo global para combatir el racismo 25 años después de Durban
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En 2001, las Naciones Unidas adoptaron la Declaración de Durban para luchar contra el racismo, la discriminación y la xenofobia en todo el mundo. Esto respondió a problemas históricos como el colonialismo y el apartheid, especialmente en Sudáfrica. Más de 20 años después, el racismo sigue siendo un problema serio, y la ONU está renovando su compromiso para eliminarlo.

**Qué pasó** – El lunes, los Estados miembros de la ONU se reunieron para renovar sus esfuerzos contra el racismo con una nueva declaración. La activista juvenil estadounidense Marley Dias habló sobre cómo muchos jóvenes nunca aprenden la verdadera historia de la esclavitud y el colonialismo. Destacó la importancia de la educación y la representación, compartiendo que comenzó la campaña #1000BlackGirlBooks a los 11 años porque no encontraba libros sobre niñas como ella. La reunión también abordó nuevos desafíos, como la rápida difusión de discursos de odio en línea, especialmente con tecnologías como la inteligencia artificial.

**Impacto** – Esta nueva declaración es importante porque reconoce que el racismo sigue siendo generalizado y cambia con la tecnología nueva. También pide acciones específicas como reparaciones por la esclavitud y el colonialismo, leyes más fuertes y educación para los jóvenes. La inclusión de voces jóvenes y el enfoque en herramientas digitales muestran una manera moderna de enfrentar el racismo. La reunión recordó que el racismo afecta a muchos grupos, incluyendo a personas de ascendencia africana, pueblos indígenas, migrantes y refugiados.

**Próximo paso** – La nueva declaración será adoptada formalmente en la Asamblea General de la ONU. El Secretario General pidió a los países que ratifiquen y apliquen completamente la Convención Internacional para la Eliminación de Todas las Formas de Discriminación Racial. La ONU también se enfocará en la Segunda Década Internacional para las Personas de Ascendencia Africana que empieza en diciembre de 2024, con el objetivo de lograr cambios reales en leyes e instituciones para detener el racismo.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Las Naciones Unidas renuevan su lucha global contra el racismo con una nueva declaración que enfatiza la educación, las reparaciones y leyes más fuertes para construir sociedades más justas.

articles.title: World News in Brief: Refugee funding, US migration policy triggers ‘cascade’ of rights violations, world forests report, restorative justice in Colombia
articles.summary: Support for water and sanitation at the biggest camp in the world for Syrian refugees is under threat from a lack of funding – combined with the impact of climate change – the UN Children’s Fund, UNICEF, said on Monday.
articles.content:
Zaatari refugee camp hosts more than 80,000 Syrians and well over half are children.

According to the agency, unless investment comes soon, its water and sanitation services could stop in a matter of months.

UNICEF regional spokesperson Louise Wateridge pointed out that many children in Zaatari had been born in the camp.

‘A lifeline’

“For them, the risk of disruption to water and sanitation services will add yet another layer of instability to lives already shaped by war and displacement. Access to safe water and sanitation remains essential for children and families who remain here,” she said.

“Until they are able to return to Syria, these services are a lifeline.”

Ms. Wateridge warned that declining rainfall, a lack of groundwater and rising demand are placing too much pressure on the water system.

For the moment, the only solution is to bore ever-deeper wells by between seven and 10 metres every year.

“We have to manage every cubic metre carefully and the plan further ahead,” the agency said, noting that its programme is 90 per cent underfunded.

Tweet URL

US migration scheme ‘triggering cascade’ of rights violations, experts warn

Independent UN human rights experts warned on Monday that the United States’ policy of sending migrants and asylum seekers to third countries is exposing people to torture, persecution and enforced disappearance.

At least 23,000 people have already been sent to 29 countries and territories, with agreements now covering 35, and the experts said more are being signed “every day”.

“The harms caused by this US Government scheme are no longer hypothetical,” they said. “The arrangements are triggering a cascade of human rights violations.”

Living in limbo

Many migrants are being transferred to places where they have no ties, and some of those countries are themselves gripped by conflict, displacement and poverty, with little capacity to protect new arrivals.

Children, women, people with disabilities, trafficking victims and LGBT people face the gravest risks, independent experts warn.

The experts also cautioned that pressure on migrants to return to their home countries cannot be considered voluntary when they are detained, penniless and without legal advice.

“States cannot contract out of their international legal obligations,” they said, calling on all governments involved to halt the arrangements immediately.

“Human rights must be at the centre of migration governance, not sacrificed in the pursuit of deterrence.”

The experts are appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, serve in an independent capacity and receive no salary for their work.

Tweet URL

Planting trees is cost-effective response to growing global challenges

The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) on Monday issued an appeal to take better care of the world’s forests as a holistic way to lay down roots against the climate crisis and hunger.

An estimated 489 million hectares of forest were lost between 1990 and 2025 through deforestation, the agency said, while more than 460 million hectares of forest are now “degraded” worldwide.

Population growth, land-use change and rising demand for natural resources are among the reasons for this change.

In a new report, FAO insists that planting trees and restoring land will also help protect vital biodiversity and rural farming communities in support of sustainable development.

Wood from the trees

One third of the world’s population depends on trees and forests for food security and work.

The agency’s State of the World’s Forests (SOFO) 2026 report warns that action at scale will require greater investment and sustained political commitment from governments if it’s to be successful.

Restoring more than one billion hectares of degraded land could generate $1.8 trillion per year in benefits, including better biodiversity, improved water courses and healthier soils.

Colombia: Türk hails ‘landmark’ restorative justice steps

UN human rights chief Volker Türk on Monday welcomed victim reparation measures in Colombia involving former FARC-EP leaders and army officers who have acknowledged responsibility for grave abuses during the country’s armed conflict.

The two former adversaries are now working side by side at a cemetery in Pitalito, Huila, searching for the disappeared so remains can be returned to their families.

The work forms part of restorative orders imposed by the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, in place of prison sentences.

“Colombia's landmark restorative measures with respect to that conflict, now underway, are a global achievement for transitional justice,” Mr. Türk said, calling the collaboration “a powerful contribution to truth, reparation, and healing” for victims and their families.

Sustained funding plea

He urged sufficient funding for the Comprehensive System for Peace. “This cannot be a one-off,” he said.

The UN has supported Colombia’s peace process since the 2016 agreement, which ended more than five decades of conflict.

The UN human rights office helped create the Comprehensive System for Peace, provided technical assistance and kept victims’ rights at the centre of the Special Jurisdiction’s work.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article reports multiple significant positive developments with broad societal impact: ongoing humanitarian support for Syrian refugees despite funding challenges, urgent UN warnings on human rights violations linked to US migration policies, a global call for forest restoration to combat climate change and hunger, and landmark restorative justice efforts in Colombia promoting peace and healing after decades of conflict. These stories highlight meaningful progress in human rights, environmental conservation, and peacebuilding with substantial real-world benefits and clear context.

articles.title: ‘Ballot must replace the bullets’, South Sudan tells General Assembly ahead of elections
articles.summary: South Sudan remains committed to holding general elections in December to conclude its transition period, the country’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Cecilia Adout Majok Adeng, told the General Assembly on Monday, calling for all sanctions, including the arms embargo to be lifted.
articles.content:
Speaking to delegations in the Assembly’s annual General Debate, Ms. Adeng said the vote would provide South Sudanese people the opportunity to choose their own leaders democratically, 15 years after the country’s independence.

She acknowledged that much work remained: electoral institutions need adequate resources, political dialogue must continue, security arrangements must advance and refugees and internally displaced persons must not be left out.

“The people of South Sudan must increasingly speak for themselves, and they must speak through the ballot […] Political competition must never again become armed confrontation. The ballot must replace the bullets,” she said.

No return to war

Ms. Adeng said South Sudan had faced internal conflict shortly after independence and that implementation of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, meant to end the second Sudanese civil war and develop democratic governance, had taken longer than anticipated.

“The government does not deny these realities,” she said, adding that the challenges should not erase the progress made.

Throughout the transitional period, she said, President Kiir had made one commitment clear – that he will “not take South Sudan back to war”.

Arguing that peaceful elections require security, she called for constructive engagement with the Security Council on restrictive measures.

“South Sudan’s objective is not militarisation,” she said, rather it was professional, unified and accountable security forces under civilian authority and the rule of law.

Sanctions should be instruments for achieving peace with clearly defined objectives, she added.

Beyond peacekeeping

While thanking the UN Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) and honouring peacekeepers who had lost their lives, Ms. Adeng said the country did not want to remain indefinitely dependent on international peacekeeping and called for greater investment in its police, judiciary, education and healthcare.

She urged international partners and investors to look beyond the country’s current challenges.

“Do not ask only what South Sudan needs, ask what South Sudan can offer,” she said.

On neighbouring Sudan, Ms. Adeng said South Sudan supported regional and international peace efforts, adding: “Even the longest conflict must eventually reach a negotiated settlement.”

She also reaffirmed support for the Common African Position on Security Council reform, noting that Africa’s Member States have no permanent seat on the Council.

To partners who supported South Sudan through its liberation struggle and independence, she said: “Stand with South Sudan again but let this chapter be a partnership.”
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article reports South Sudan's commitment to holding democratic elections to end its transitional period and replace armed conflict with peaceful political processes. This represents a significant positive step toward peace, democratic governance, and human rights for a country long affected by civil war. The call to lift sanctions to facilitate security and the emphasis on inclusive participation and institutional development further underline the meaningful impact and broad significance for the South Sudanese people and the region.
articles.personality_title: South Sudan commits to peaceful elections to end transition period
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – South Sudan gained independence 15 years ago but has faced ongoing conflict and delays in establishing stable government. The country is currently in a transitional phase, moving towards its first general elections.

**What happened** – On Monday, South Sudan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Cecilia Adout Majok Adeng, told the UN General Assembly that the country is determined to hold general elections this December. She asked for all sanctions, including an arms embargo, to be lifted to help ensure security during the elections. Ms. Adeng emphasized that the elections will allow South Sudanese people to choose their leaders peacefully instead of through violence.

**Impact** – This commitment marks an important step away from years of armed conflict. Holding elections means South Sudan aims to replace fighting with democratic processes. The focus on including refugees and displaced people shows a push for fairness and broad participation. Asking for fewer sanctions signals a desire to build strong, professional security forces under civilian control, which is key to lasting peace.

**What's next step** – South Sudan will work on preparing electoral institutions and continuing political dialogue in the coming months. The country also plans to strengthen its police, courts, schools, and healthcare systems so it can rely less on international peacekeepers. International partners are encouraged to support South Sudan not just for its needs but for its potential contributions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – South Sudan is taking important steps to end conflict by holding democratic elections and building peaceful, inclusive institutions.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le Soudan du Sud s'engage à des élections pacifiques pour clore sa période de transition
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le Soudan du Sud a obtenu son indépendance il y a 15 ans, mais a connu des conflits et des retards dans l'établissement d'un gouvernement stable. Le pays est actuellement en phase de transition, en vue de ses premières élections générales.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Lundi, la représentante permanente du Soudan du Sud auprès des Nations unies, Cecilia Adout Majok Adeng, a déclaré à l'Assemblée générale de l'ONU que le pays est déterminé à organiser des élections générales en décembre. Elle a demandé la levée de toutes les sanctions, y compris l'embargo sur les armes, pour garantir la sécurité pendant les élections. Mme Adeng a souligné que ces élections permettront au peuple soudanais du Sud de choisir ses dirigeants pacifiquement, plutôt que par la violence.

**Impact** – Cet engagement représente une étape importante pour sortir des années de conflit armé. Organiser des élections signifie que le Soudan du Sud veut remplacer les combats par des processus démocratiques. L'accent mis sur l'inclusion des réfugiés et des déplacés montre une volonté d'équité et de large participation. La demande de levée des sanctions reflète le désir de construire des forces de sécurité solides et professionnelles sous contrôle civil, essentiel pour une paix durable.

**Prochaine étape** – Le Soudan du Sud va préparer les institutions électorales et poursuivre le dialogue politique dans les mois à venir. Le pays prévoit aussi de renforcer sa police, sa justice, ses écoles et ses soins de santé pour dépendre moins des casques bleus internationaux. articles.personality_title_es: Sudán del Sur se compromete a elecciones pacíficas para finalizar su periodo de transición
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Sudán del Sur logró su independencia hace 15 años, pero ha enfrentado conflictos y retrasos para establecer un gobierno estable. Actualmente está en una fase de transición hacia sus primeras elecciones generales.

**Qué pasó** – El lunes, Cecilia Adout Majok Adeng, representante permanente de Sudán del Sur ante la ONU, dijo a la Asamblea General que el país está decidido a realizar elecciones generales en diciembre. Pidió que se levanten todas las sanciones, incluyendo el embargo de armas, para ayudar a garantizar la seguridad durante las elecciones. Ms. Adeng destacó que los comicios permitirán a la gente elegir líderes de forma pacífica en lugar de con violencia.

**Impacto** – Este compromiso es un paso importante para dejar atrás años de conflicto armado. Realizar elecciones significa que Sudán del Sur quiere sustituir la lucha por procesos democráticos. El enfoque en incluir a refugiados y desplazados muestra un esfuerzo por la justicia y la participación amplia. La petición para reducir sanciones refleja el deseo de construir fuerzas de seguridad profesionales bajo control civil, clave para una paz duradera.

**Próximo paso** – Sudán del Sur trabajará en preparar las instituciones electorales y continuar el diálogo político en los próximos meses. También planea fortalecer su policía, tribunales, escuelas y servicios de salud para depender menos de los cascos azules internacionales. Se anima a los socios internacionales a apoyar a Sudán del Sur no solo por sus necesidades, sino por lo que puede ofrecer.

**Frase clave** – Sudán del Sur avanza para terminar el conflicto mediante elecciones democráticas y la construcción de instituciones pacíficas e inclusivas.

articles.title: Biodiversity protection must include language preservation
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03056-5Biodiversity protection must include language preservation
articles.content:
The loss of an Indigenous language can also mean the loss of the ecological and medicinal knowledge embedded in it (see R. Cámara-Leret et al. Nature 655, 1212–1216; 2026). Although declines in language use can be reversed, efforts to do so remain overlooked in national legislation and policies. Governments should provide sustained support for community-led immersion, family- and land-based learning and digital tools that help speakers to teach and pass on their languages to the next generation.

Nature 658, 286 (2026)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03056-5

articles.personality_title: Preserving Indigenous languages helps protect nature’s knowledge
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many Indigenous languages are disappearing around the world. When these languages are lost, important knowledge about plants, animals, and medicine that people have passed down for generations can disappear too.

**What happened** – Scientists and experts have pointed out that saving Indigenous languages is closely connected to protecting the environment. They say governments should support programs that help communities teach their languages to young people. This can include learning at home, in nature, and using technology.

**Impact** – This idea is important because Indigenous languages carry unique information about local plants and animals that might be unknown to others. Protecting these languages helps keep this knowledge alive, which can help with caring for the environment and finding new medicines.

**What's next step** – Governments and organizations are encouraged to create laws and give ongoing support for language programs led by Indigenous communities. Using digital tools and land-based learning will be key in helping younger generations learn and use their native languages.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Saving Indigenous languages is a vital step in protecting both cultural heritage and the natural world’s hidden wisdom.
